stem: A bank offers two schemes on a deposit of Rs 20,000 for 2 years: Scheme A pays 10% per annum simple interest; Scheme B pays 9.5% per annum compounded annually. Which scheme gives a higher return and by how much? [Given: (1.095)^2 = 1.199025]

per_option_rationale.rationale: A higher nominal rate under SI can outperform a lower rate under CI over short horizons; do not assume compounding always wins.
Choosing Scheme B incorrectly assumes compounding always beats simple interest regardless of rate; here the SI rate (10%) is high enough that SI returns more than CI at 9.5% over 2 years.

Rs 180.50 comes from subtracting Scheme B interest of Rs 3819.50 from an incorrectly computed Scheme A interest of Rs 4000, confusing 20000 x 0.10 x 2 correctly but misreading Scheme B factor as 1.1900 instead of 1.199025, giving 20000 x 0.19 = 3800 and a difference of 200, further rounded to 180.50.
Stating both are equal misapplies the equivalence formula for effective annual rate; 10% SI and 9.5% CI are only numerically equal when n = 1, not n = 2.

explanation_sections.punchline: A higher nominal rate under SI can outperform a lower rate under CI over short horizons; do not assume compounding always wins.
explanation_sections.lesson: When comparing SI vs CI across schemes, always compute both returns numerically rather than assuming CI dominates. The crossover depends on both rate and horizon.
explanation_sections.timing: 90 seconds: compute SI in one step (flat multiplication), CI in one step using the hint, then subtract. Trap is option 2; the distractor banks on the reflex that compounding beats simple interest.
